title: Ἑλένη ἐπὶ πύργον
titleEn: Helen Comes to the Tower — Iliad 3.84–170
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Agamemnon’s order to stop is obeyed, and Hector tells both armies that Alexander offers to fight Menelaus alone for Helen and all the possessions, with oaths for the rest. Menelaus agrees and asks for two lambs for Earth and the Sun, one for Zeus, and Priam himself to swear, since a young man’s wits flutter while an old man looks ahead and behind. Both armies are glad, lay down their arms, and send heralds for the lambs and for Priam. Iris, in the likeness of Laodice, finds Helen weaving the struggles fought for her and calls her to see the armies sitting quiet; a longing for her first husband, her city and her parents comes over Helen, and she goes with two handmaids to the Scaean Gates. There the old men of Troy, like cicadas in a tree, say softly that no one can blame the war over such a woman, though she should go home in the ships; Priam calls her to sit beside him and name the huge Achaean man.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἔσχοντο μάχης ἄνεῴ τ’ ἐγένοντο
ἐσσυμένως·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ eschonto machēs aneōi t’ egenonto
essymenōs·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they held themselves back from the fighting and became speechless,
hurriedly;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and in haste they held back from the fighting and fell speechless;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the stock ‘so he spoke’, here closing Agamemnon’s speech of 82–83; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with the τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἳ. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the two armies. ἔσχοντο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘held themselves back’, with the genitive μάχης ‘from the fighting’. ἄνεῴ is the nominative plural of ἀνεώς ‘speechless’, so ἄνεῴ τ’ ἐγένοντο is ‘and became speechless’. ἐσσυμένως ‘hurriedly’ is the adverb of the participle ἐσσύμενος (from σεύομαι ‘hurry’); it stands alone at the start of line 85 and goes with both verbs.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δὲ μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: Hektōr de met’ amphoteroisin eeipe·
sentences.l: and Hector among both spoke:
sentences.i: and Hector spoke among them both:
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ δὲ … ἔειπε introduces the first speech of the part, which begins in the next unit. μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν is ‘among both’, μετά with the dative, and ‘both’ means both armies, who have just fallen silent. ἔειπε is the epic form of the aorist εἶπε ‘said’.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
μῦθον Ἀλεξάνδροιο, τοῦ εἵνεκα νεῖκος ὄρωρεν.
sentences.tr:
keklyte meu Trōes kai eÿknēmides Achaioi
mython Alexandroio, tou heineka neikos orōren.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans,
the word of Alexander, for whose sake the quarrel has arisen.
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans, the word of Alexander, for whose sake the quarrel has arisen.
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with the genitive μευ (epic for μου) ‘me’ for the person heard and the accusative μῦθον ‘word’ for what is heard. ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί is the stock ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ (greaves are shin-guards). Ἀλεξάνδροιο has the epic genitive -οιο; Alexander is Paris, whose proposal Hector goes on to report. τοῦ εἵνεκα is ‘for whose sake’ (εἵνεκα is the epic form of ἕνεκα), and ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘has arisen’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλους μὲν κέλεται Τρῶας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
τεύχεα κάλ’ ἀποθέσθαι ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ,
αὐτὸν δ’ ἐν μέσσῳ καὶ ἀρηΐφιλον Μενέλαον
οἴους ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ καὶ κτήμασι πᾶσι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
allous men keletai Trōas kai pantas Achaious
teuchea kal’ apothesthai epi chthoni poulyboteirēi,
auton d’ en messōi kai arēïphilon Menelaon
oious amph’ Helenēi kai ktēmasi pasi machesthai.
sentences.l:
The others, he bids, Trojans and all Achaeans,
to lay down their fine armour on the much-nourishing earth,
and himself in the middle and Ares-loved Menelaus,
alone, to fight over Helen and all the possessions.
sentences.i: He bids the rest of the Trojans and all the Achaeans lay down their fine armour on the earth that feeds so many, and he himself and Menelaus, dear to Ares, fight alone in the middle for Helen and all the possessions.
sentences.n: κέλεται ‘he bids’ (Alexander is the subject, as in 87) governs two infinitives with their subjects in the accusative: ἄλλους … Τρῶας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιούς ‘the others, Trojans and all Achaeans’ with ἀποθέσθαι ‘to lay down’ (aorist middle of ἀποτίθημι), and αὐτὸν … καὶ … Μενέλαον ‘himself and Menelaus’ with μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’, οἴους ‘alone’ agreeing with them. ἄλλους μέν … αὐτὸν δέ sets the many against the two. κάλ’ is καλά ‘fine’, and πουλυβοτείρῃ is the epic form of πολυβοτείρῃ, the stock ‘much-nourishing’ said of the earth. ἀρηΐφιλον is the stock ‘Ares-loved’, ‘dear to Ares’, of Menelaus. ἀμφ’ Ἑλένῃ καὶ κτήμασι πᾶσι is ‘over Helen and all the possessions’.

sentences.t:
ὁππότερος δέ κε νικήσῃ κρείσσων τε γένηται
κτήμαθ’ ἑλὼν εὖ πάντα γυναῖκά τε οἴκαδ’ ἀγέσθω·
sentences.tr:
hoppoteros de ke nikēsēi kreissōn te genētai
ktēmath’ helōn eu panta gynaika te oikad’ agesthō·
sentences.l:
and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger,
the possessions having taken, well, all, and the woman, home let him lead;
sentences.i: and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger, let him properly take all the possessions and lead the woman home;
sentences.n: These two lines are word for word the two of Alexander’s own speech at 71–72, which Hector now passes on in Alexander’s words; the edition prints no comma after γένηται here, as it does at 71. ὁππότερος is ‘whichever of two’, with νικήσῃ and γένηται in the subjunctive after κε. κτήμαθ’ is κτήματα ‘possessions’, and ἑλών the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘having taken’. εὖ ‘well, properly’ is joined to ἑλών, and ἀγέσθω is the middle imperative of ἄγω, ‘let him lead (for himself), take home’; οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with the -δε of direction.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμωμεν.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ alloi philotēta kai horkia pista tamōmen.
sentences.l: and we others, friendship and faithful oaths let us cut.”
sentences.i: and let the rest of us make friendship and swear faithful oaths.”
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and we others’: the verb is first person plural, τάμωμεν, the aorist subjunctive of τέμνω ‘cut’ used as an exhortation, ‘let us cut’, so this οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι includes the speaker, where Alexander’s same opening words at 73 were ‘you others’. φιλότητα καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμωμεν is ‘let us cut friendship and faithful oaths’; ‘cutting’ oaths comes from cutting the victims. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ closes Hector’s speech, as it closed Agamemnon’s at 84. οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες is ‘and they then all’. ἀκήν is an adverb, ‘still, hushed’, and σιωπῇ the dative ‘in silence’; ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is a set phrase, ‘became still in silence’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe boēn agathos Menelaos·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: And Menelaus, good at the war-cry, also spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the article as a pronoun, ‘to them’, and with μετέειπε (the aorist of μετεῖπον ‘speak among’) gives ‘spoke among them’; καί ‘also’ marks a second speaker after Hector. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus, βοήν being an accusative of respect. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε νῦν καὶ ἐμεῖο·
sentences.tr: keklyte nyn kai emeio·
sentences.l: “Hear now me, too;
sentences.i: “Hear me, too, now;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, as in Hector’s κέκλυτέ μευ at 86. ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ ‘me’, the person heard, and καί ‘also’ goes with it: Menelaus asks to be heard after Hector.

sentences.t:
μάλιστα γὰρ ἄλγος ἱκάνει
θυμὸν ἐμόν, φρονέω δὲ διακρινθήμεναι ἤδη
Ἀργείους καὶ Τρῶας, ἐπεὶ κακὰ πολλὰ πέπασθε
εἵνεκ’ ἐμῆς ἔριδος καὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ’ ἀρχῆς·
sentences.tr:
malista gar algos hikanei
thymon emon, phroneō de diakrinthēmenai ēdē
Argeious kai Trōas, epei kaka polla pepasthe
heinek’ emēs eridos kai Alexandrou henek’ archēs·
sentences.l:
for most of all pain reaches
my heart, and I am minded that they be parted now,
Argives and Trojans, since many evils you have suffered
because of my strife and for the sake of Alexander’s beginning;
sentences.i: for pain comes upon my heart most of all, and I think Argives and Trojans should now be parted, since you have suffered many evils because of my strife and of the beginning Alexander made;
sentences.n: μάλιστα γάρ ‘for most of all’ gives the reason he asks to be heard. ἄλγος ‘pain’ is the subject of ἱκάνει ‘reaches’, with θυμὸν ἐμόν ‘my heart’ as what it reaches. φρονέω δὲ διακρινθήμεναι ἤδη is ‘and I am minded that they be parted now’: φρονέω ‘think, be minded’ takes the aorist passive infinitive διακρινθήμεναι (epic -ήμεναι, Attic -ῆναι) ‘to be parted’, whose subject Ἀργείους καὶ Τρῶας stands in the accusative. πέπασθε is the epic perfect of πάσχω ‘suffer’ (Attic πεπόνθατε), ‘you have suffered’. In εἵνεκ’ ἐμῆς ἔριδος ‘because of my strife’ and Ἀλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ’ ἀρχῆς the second ἕνεκ’ (epic ἕνεκα) stands between the noun and its genitive: ‘for the sake of Alexander’s beginning’. ἀρχή here is the start of the wrong, the beginning Alexander made; the word can also mean ‘rule’, which does not suit.

sentences.t:
ἡμέων δ’ ὁπποτέρῳ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα τέτυκται
τεθναίη·
sentences.tr:
hēmeōn d’ hoppoterōi thanatos kai moira tetyktai
tethnaiē·
sentences.l:
and of us two, for whichever death and fate has been made ready,
let him be dead;
sentences.i: and for whichever of us two death and fate have been made ready, let him be dead;
sentences.n: ἡμέων is the epic genitive plural of ἐγώ ‘of us’, and ὁπποτέρῳ ‘for whichever of two’ is a dative of the person concerned, so ‘of us two’ means Menelaus and Alexander. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make, prepare’, singular with its two subjects θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα ‘death and fate’. τεθναίη is the perfect optative of θνῄσκω, ‘may he be dead’, a wish that works as a command.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι δὲ διακρινθεῖτε τάχιστα.
sentences.tr: alloi de diakrintheite tachista.
sentences.l: and you others, may you be parted most quickly.
sentences.i: and may the rest of you be parted as quickly as possible.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι ‘others’ is the rest of the two armies, spoken to directly. διακρινθεῖτε is the aorist passive optative of διακρίνω ‘part’, second person plural, an optative that does the work of a command, ‘may you be parted’; τάχιστα is the superlative adverb of ταχύς, ‘most quickly’.

sentences.t:
οἴσετε ἄρν’, ἕτερον λευκόν, ἑτέρην δὲ μέλαιναν,
Γῇ τε καὶ Ἠελίῳ·
sentences.tr:
oisete arn’, heteron leukon, heterēn de melainan,
Gēi te kai Ēeliōi·
sentences.l:
Bring two lambs, one white, and the other black,
for Earth and Sun;
sentences.i: Bring two lambs, one white and the other black, for Earth and the Sun;
sentences.n: οἴσετε is a plural command, ‘bring’ (the stem οἰσ- belongs to φέρω). ἄρν’ is the dual ἄρνε ‘two lambs’ with its last vowel elided, as the words that follow show: ἕτερον λευκόν ‘the one white’ and ἑτέρην δὲ μέλαιναν ‘but the other black’, the first masculine in form and the second feminine, so a male and a female lamb. Γῇ is the dative of Γαῖα ‘Earth’ and Ἠελίῳ the dative of Ἠέλιος ‘the Sun’ (the epic form of Ἥλιος): the two powers to whom the first pair of victims go.

sentences.t: Διὶ δ’ ἡμεῖς οἴσομεν ἄλλον·
sentences.tr: Dii d’ hēmeis oisomen allon·
sentences.l: and for Zeus we will bring another;
sentences.i: and for Zeus we will bring another;
sentences.n: Διὶ δ’ is ‘and for Zeus’. ἡμεῖς ‘we’ is expressed to set Menelaus’ own side against those told to bring the first two; οἴσομεν is the future ‘we will bring’, and ἄλλον ‘another’ is a third victim, masculine in form, for Zeus.

sentences.t:
ἄξετε δὲ Πριάμοιο βίην, ὄφρ’ ὅρκια τάμνῃ
αὐτός, ἐπεί οἱ παῖδες ὑπερφίαλοι καὶ ἄπιστοι,
μή τις ὑπερβασίῃ Διὸς ὅρκια δηλήσηται.
sentences.tr:
axete de Priamoio biēn, ophr’ horkia tamnēi
autos, epei hoi paides hyperphialoi kai apistoi,
mē tis hyperbasiēi Dios horkia dēlēsētai.
sentences.l:
And bring the might of Priam, so that the oaths he may cut
himself, since his sons are overweening and faithless,
lest anyone through overstepping the oaths of Zeus harm.
sentences.i: And bring the might of Priam, so that he may cut the oaths himself, since his sons are overweening and faithless, lest anyone through overstepping do harm to the oaths of Zeus.
sentences.n: ἄξετε ‘bring’ is a plural command like οἴσετε in 103, here of a person (ἄγω). Πριάμοιο βίην ‘the might of Priam’ is a periphrasis for Priam himself, and both layers keep it. ὄφρα with the subjunctive τάμνῃ is ‘so that he may cut’, and αὐτός ‘himself’ stresses that Priam, not his sons, must swear. οἱ is the dative of the third-person pronoun, ‘his’; ὑπερφίαλοι ‘overweening’ and ἄπιστοι ‘faithless’ (ἀ- ‘not’ + πίστις ‘faith’) are the reasons. μή τις … δηλήσηται is a fear or purpose clause, ‘lest anyone harm’: δηλέομαι is ‘harm, damage’ and ὑπερβασίῃ ‘by overstepping’ is the dative of the means; Διὸς ὅρκια ‘the oaths of Zeus’ are the oaths sworn by him.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δ’ ὁπλοτέρων ἀνδρῶν φρένες ἠερέθονται·
sentences.tr: aiei d’ hoploterōn andrōn phrenes ēerethontai·
sentences.l: for always of younger men the wits are fluttering;
sentences.i: for the wits of younger men are always fluttering;
sentences.n: αἰεί is ‘always’, and ὁπλοτέρων is the genitive plural of ὁπλότερος ‘younger’. φρένες ‘wits’ is the subject of ἠερέθονται, from the rare verb ἠερέθομαι ‘hang waving, flutter’ (it is said of the aegis’s tassels at 2.448); of the wits it means ‘are unsteady, blown about’. The sentence gives the reason Menelaus wants Priam, an old man, to swear.

sentences.t:
οἷς δ’ ὁ γέρων μετέῃσιν ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω
λεύσσει, ὅπως ὄχ’ ἄριστα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι γένηται.
sentences.tr:
hois d’ ho gerōn meteēisin hama prossō kai opissō
leussei, hopōs och’ arista met’ amphoteroisi genētai.
sentences.l:
but among whom the old man is, at once forward and backward
he looks, how by far the best among both may come about.”
sentences.i: but where an old man is among them, he looks at what lies ahead and what lies behind, so that it may turn out far best for both sides.”
sentences.n: οἷς δ’ is ‘but among whom’, the dative of the relative; μετέῃσιν is the epic subjunctive of μέτειμι ‘be among’, standing without κε in a general clause (‘wherever the old man is among them’). ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ has the article in its old sense of ‘that’ man. ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω λεύσσει is ‘he looks at once forward and backward’, ahead to what will follow and behind to what has been. ὅπως with the subjunctive γένηται is ‘how it may come about’, a purpose; ὄχ’ ἄριστα is ‘by far the best’, and μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι ‘among both’ is both sides, as at 85. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἐχάρησαν Ἀχαιοί τε Τρῶές τε
ἐλπόμενοι παύσασθαι ὀϊζυροῦ πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ echarēsan Achaioi te Trōes te
elpomenoi pausasthai oïzyrou polemoio.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they rejoiced, Achaeans and Trojans both,
hoping to cease from sorrowful war.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Achaeans and Trojans both were glad, hoping to cease from sorrowful war.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the stock ‘so he spoke’, closing Menelaus’ speech. ἐχάρησαν is the aorist of χαίρω ‘rejoiced’. Ἀχαιοί τε Τρῶές τε is ‘both Achaeans and Trojans’, and ἐλπόμενοι ‘hoping’ takes the aorist middle infinitive παύσασθαι ‘to cease’, with the genitive ὀϊζυροῦ πολέμοιο ‘from sorrowful war’. ὀϊζυρός ‘sorrowful’ is the adjective of ὀϊζύς ‘sorrow’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἵππους μὲν ἔρυξαν ἐπὶ στίχας, ἐκ δ’ ἔβαν αὐτοί,
τεύχεά τ’ ἐξεδύοντο·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ hippous men eryxan epi stichas, ek d’ eban autoi,
teuchea t’ exedyonto·
sentences.l:
And then the horses they held back along the ranks, and out they stepped themselves,
and their armour they were taking off;
sentences.i: Then they held the horses back along the ranks, got out themselves, and took off their armour;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ is καὶ ἄρα ‘and then’. ἔρυξαν is the aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, with ἐπὶ στίχας ‘along the ranks’ (στίχες are lines of men). ἐκ δ’ ἔβαν is ἐκ … ἔβησαν (tmesis), ‘and out they went’: the Greek does not name the chariots they stepped out of, and αὐτοί ‘themselves’ sets the men against the horses. ἐξεδύοντο is the imperfect middle of ἐκδύω, ‘were taking off’, with τεύχεα ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
τὰ μὲν κατέθεντ’ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
πλησίον ἀλλήλων, ὀλίγη δ’ ἦν ἀμφὶς ἄρουρα·
sentences.tr:
ta men katethent’ epi gaiēi
plēsion allēlōn, oligē d’ ēn amphis aroura·
sentences.l:
these they laid down upon the earth
near one another, and small was the plough-land between;
sentences.i: They laid the armour down on the ground close to one another, and little plough-land lay between;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν ‘these’ points back to τεύχεα ‘armour’; the μέν is answered by the δέ of ὀλίγη δ’. κατέθεντ’ is κατέθεντο, the aorist middle of κατατίθημι ‘lay down’. πλησίον ἀλλήλων is ‘near one another’, with the genitive. ἀμφίς is ‘on both sides’ and so ‘between’, and ἄρουρα is ‘plough-land’, the field between the two armies.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ προτὶ ἄστυ δύω κήρυκας ἔπεμπε
καρπαλίμως ἄρνάς τε φέρειν Πρίαμόν τε καλέσσαι·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr de proti asty dyō kērykas epempe
karpalimōs arnas te pherein Priamon te kalessai·
sentences.l:
And Hector toward the town two heralds sent
swiftly, both lambs to bring and Priam to call;
sentences.i: And Hector sent two heralds swiftly to the town, to bring the lambs and to call Priam;
sentences.n: προτί is the epic form of πρός ‘toward’, ἄστυ is ‘town’, and δύω is ‘two’. ἔπεμπε is the imperfect of πέμπω ‘send’. The two infinitives φέρειν ‘to bring’ and καλέσσαι ‘to call’ (aorist, with the epic doubled σσ) say what the heralds are sent to do, ἄρνάς τε … Πρίαμόν τε ‘both the lambs and Priam’. καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ Ταλθύβιον προΐει κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυρὰς ἰέναι, ἠδ’ ἄρν’ ἐκέλευεν
οἰσέμεναι·
sentences.tr:
autar ho Talthybion proïei kreiōn Agamemnōn
nēas epi glaphyras ienai, ēd’ arn’ ekeleuen
oisemenai·
sentences.i: But lord Agamemnon sent Talthybius to the hollow ships, and ordered that a lamb be brought;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’, picked up by the apposition κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘lord Agamemnon’ at the end of the line. Ταλθύβιον is Agamemnon’s herald (he is named at 1.320). προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’, and νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is ‘to the hollow ships’, with ἔπι standing after its noun; ἰέναι ‘to go’ says the purpose. ἄρν’ here is ἄρνα, one lamb, the one for Zeus (104); the elided form could also be the dual of 103, but Hector’s heralds are already sent for the lambs of the first pair (117), and the third victim is the Achaeans’ to bring. ἐκέλευεν is the imperfect ‘he ordered’ and οἰσέμεναι the future infinitive in -έμεναι, ‘to bring’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ οὐκ ἀπίθησ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ar’ ouk apithēs’ Agamemnoni diōi.
sentences.l: and he then did not disobey heavenly Agamemnon.
sentences.i: and he did not disobey heavenly Agamemnon.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Talthybius. ἀπίθησ’ is ἀπίθησε, the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’, with the dative. Ἀγαμέμνονι δίῳ is ‘heavenly Agamemnon’, δῖος being the stock epithet that is translated each time.

sentences.t:
Ἶρις δ’ αὖθ’ Ἑλένῃ λευκωλένῳ ἄγγελος ἦλθεν
εἰδομένη γαλόῳ Ἀντηνορίδαο δάμαρτι,
τὴν Ἀντηνορίδης εἶχε κρείων Ἑλικάων
Λαοδίκην Πριάμοιο θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστην.
sentences.tr:
Iris d’ auth’ Helenēi leukōlenōi angelos ēlthen
eidomenē galoōi Antēnoridao damarti,
tēn Antēnoridēs eiche kreiōn Helikaōn
Laodikēn Priamoio thygatrōn eidos aristēn.
sentences.l:
And Iris in turn to white-armed Helen as messenger came,
making herself like her husband’s sister, the wife of Antenor’s son,
whom Antenor’s son had, lord Helicaon,
Laodice, of Priam’s daughters in form the best.
sentences.i: And Iris came as messenger to white-armed Helen, making herself like her husband’s sister, the wife of Antenor’s son: Laodice, the best in form of Priam’s daughters, whom the son of Antenor, lord Helicaon, had as his wife.
sentences.n: Ἶρις δ’ αὖθ’ is ‘and Iris in turn’ (αὖθ’ is a form of αὖτε/αὖθις ‘again, in turn’), and ἄγγελος ‘messenger’ says her role. λευκωλένῳ ‘white-armed’ is the stock epithet of Helen. εἰδομένη is the participle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’, with the dative γαλόῳ (γάλως, a husband’s sister) and δάμαρτι ‘wife’: Laodice, a daughter of Priam, is Alexander’s sister and therefore Helen’s husband’s sister. Ἀντηνορίδαο is the epic genitive and Ἀντηνορίδης the nominative of ‘Antenor’s son’; the second is Helicaon. εἶχε is the imperfect of ἔχω, ‘had’, here ‘had as wife’. κρείων ‘lord’ is the stock word as in κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων. εἶδος is an accusative of respect, ‘in form’, with ἀρίστην ‘best’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ εὗρ’ ἐν μεγάρῳ·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ heur’ en megarōi·
sentences.l: Her she found in the hall;
sentences.i: She found her in the hall;
sentences.n: τὴν ‘her’ is Helen. εὗρ’ is εὗρε, the aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, with Iris as its subject. μέγαρον is ‘hall’, the great room of a house.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ μέγαν ἱστὸν ὕφαινε
δίπλακα πορφυρέην, πολέας δ’ ἐνέπασσεν ἀέθλους
Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων,
οὕς ἑθεν εἵνεκ’ ἔπασχον ὑπ’ Ἄρηος παλαμάων·
sentences.tr:
hē de megan histon hyphaine
diplaka porphyreēn, poleas d’ enepassen aethlous
Trōōn th’ hippodamōn kai Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn,
hous hethen heinek’ epaschon hyp’ Arēos palamaōn·
sentences.l:
and she was weaving a great web,
a double cloak, purple, and many struggles she was working into it
of the horse-taming Trojans and the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
which for her sake they were suffering at the hands of Ares;
sentences.i: She was weaving a great web, a double cloak of purple, and working into it the many struggles of the Trojans, tamers of horses, and the bronze-shirted Achaeans, which they were suffering for her sake at the hands of Ares;
sentences.n: ἣ δὲ ‘and she’ is Helen. ἱστόν is ‘web’, the cloth on the loom, with μέγαν ‘great’, and δίπλακα πορφυρέην ‘double (folded) purple cloak’ says what the web is. ἐνέπασσεν is the imperfect of ἐμπάσσω, ‘was working into it’, of figures woven or embroidered into cloth; πολέας is the epic form of πολλούς ‘many’. ἀέθλους are ‘struggles’, here the fighting itself, not contests in games. Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων has the stock epithets ‘horse-taming’ and ‘bronze-shirted’ and is repeated word for word at 131. οὕς ‘which’ is the struggles; ἕθεν is the epic genitive of the third-person pronoun, ‘of her’, so ἕθεν εἵνεκ’ is ‘for her sake’ (εἵνεκ’ stands after its word). ἔπασχον is the imperfect of πάσχω ‘suffer’. ὑπ’ Ἄρηος παλαμάων is ‘at the hands of Ares’, παλαμάων the epic genitive plural of παλάμη ‘palm, hand’; Ares stands for war and the figure is kept.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē prosephē podas ōkea Iris·
sentences.l: And standing close by, swift-in-feet Iris spoke;
sentences.i: Iris, swift of foot, came and stood close by, and spoke;
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη is ‘and standing close by’, the stock opening of a message (the same words, with Athena, stand in the Odyssey, and with Iris at 2.790). προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις is ‘swift-in-feet Iris’: πόδας is an accusative of respect and ὠκέα the feminine of ὠκύς, as in Achilles’ πόδας ὠκύς. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
δεῦρ’ ἴθι νύμφα φίλη, ἵνα θέσκελα ἔργα ἴδηαι
Τρώων θ’ ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων,
οἳ πρὶν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι φέρον πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα
ἐν πεδίῳ ὀλοοῖο λιλαιόμενοι πολέμοιο·
sentences.tr:
deur’ ithi nympha philē, hina theskela erga idēai
Trōōn th’ hippodamōn kai Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn,
hoi prin ep’ allēloisi pheron polydakryn Arēa
en pediōi olooio lilaiomenoi polemoio·
sentences.l:
“Come here, dear bride, so that you may see the marvellous deeds
of the horse-taming Trojans and the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
who before against one another were bringing tearful Ares
in the plain, longing for baneful war;
sentences.i: “Come here, dear lady, to see the marvellous deeds of the Trojans, tamers of horses, and the bronze-shirted Achaeans, who before were bringing tearful battle upon one another in the plain, eager for baneful war;
sentences.n: δεῦρ’ ἴθι is ‘come here’ (ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’). νύμφα is the vocative of νύμφη ‘young wife, bride’, a warm title of address, rendered ‘lady’ in i. ἵνα with the subjunctive ἴδηαι (the second-person middle, the uncontracted form of ἴδῃ) is ‘so that you may see’. θέσκελα ‘marvellous’ is a word whose meaning is not known; the English keeps the traditional sense. The next line is the same as 127. οἳ πρὶν … φέρον is ‘who before were bringing’ (φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect), with Ἄρηα, the accusative of Ares, standing for battle, and πολύδακρυν ‘tearful’ (πολύ- ‘much’ + δάκρυ ‘tear’). λιλαιόμενοι is the participle of λιλαίομαι ‘long for’, with the genitive ὀλοοῖο πολέμοιο ‘baneful war’ (ὀλοός ‘baneful’).

sentences.t:
οἳ δὴ νῦν ἕαται σιγῇ, πόλεμος δὲ πέπαυται,
ἀσπίσι κεκλιμένοι, παρὰ δ’ ἔγχεα μακρὰ πέπηγεν.
sentences.tr:
hoi dē nyn heatai sigēi, polemos de pepautai,
aspisi keklimenoi, para d’ enchea makra pepēgen.
sentences.l:
who now sit in silence, and the war has ceased,
leaning on their shields, and beside them long spears are fixed.
sentences.i: They now sit in silence, the war has stopped, and they lean on their shields with their long spears planted beside them.
sentences.n: ἕαται is the epic third-person plural of the perfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; σιγῇ is ‘in silence’, and πέπαυται is the perfect passive of παύω, ‘has been stopped, has ceased’. κεκλιμένοι is the perfect participle of κλίνω ‘lean’, with the dative ἀσπίσι ‘on shields’. In παρὰ δ’ ἔγχεα μακρὰ πέπηγεν the neuter plural ἔγχεα ‘spears’ takes a singular verb, πέπηγεν, the perfect of πήγνυμι ‘fix’: ‘stand fixed’ in the ground. παρά is ‘beside’ (them), standing as an adverb.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀλέξανδρος καὶ ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος
μακρῇς ἐγχείῃσι μαχήσονται περὶ σεῖο·
sentences.tr:
autar Alexandros kai arēïphilos Menelaos
makrēis encheiēisi machēsontai peri seio·
sentences.l:
but Alexander and Ares-loved Menelaus
with long spears will fight about you;
sentences.i: but Alexander and Menelaus, dear to Ares, will fight with their long spears for you;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘but’, setting the two fighters against the army that sits. ἀρηΐφιλος ‘Ares-loved’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus. μακρῇς is the epic form of μακραῖς, and ἐγχείῃσι is the epic dative plural of ἐγχείη ‘spear’. μαχήσονται is the future ‘will fight’, and περὶ σεῖο is ‘about you’, σεῖο being the epic genitive of σύ.

sentences.t: τῷ δέ κε νικήσαντι φίλη κεκλήσῃ ἄκοιτις.
sentences.tr: tōi de ke nikēsanti philē keklēsēi akoitis.
sentences.l: and to him who has won, dear wife you will be called.”
sentences.i: and you will be called the dear wife of the one who wins.”
sentences.n: τῷ … νικήσαντι is a dative, ‘to him who has won’ (aorist participle), with κε making it conditional, ‘whoever wins’. κεκλήσῃ is the future perfect passive of καλέω (= κεκλήσεαι), ‘you will be called’, and ἄκοιτις is ‘wife’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰποῦσα θεὰ γλυκὺν ἵμερον ἔμβαλε θυμῷ
ἀνδρός τε προτέρου καὶ ἄστεος ἠδὲ τοκήων·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipousa thea glykyn himeron embale thymōi
andros te proterou kai asteos ēde tokēōn·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, the goddess sweet longing cast into her heart
for her former husband, and city, and parents;
sentences.i: So the goddess spoke, and put a sweet longing into Helen’s heart for her former husband, her city and her parents;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσα is ‘so having spoken’, the aorist participle of εἶπον. ἵμερον is ‘longing’, the object of ἔμβαλε (the aorist of ἐμβάλλω ‘throw in, put in’), with θυμῷ ‘in the heart’; the object of the longing is in the genitive, ἀνδρός … προτέρου καὶ ἄστεος ἠδὲ τοκήων. προτέρου ‘former’ is Menelaus, her husband before Alexander, ἄστεος is the epic genitive of ἄστυ ‘town’, and τοκήων is the epic genitive plural of τοκεύς ‘parent’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἀργεννῇσι καλυψαμένη ὀθόνῃσιν
ὁρμᾶτ’ ἐκ θαλάμοιο τέρεν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα
οὐκ οἴη, ἅμα τῇ γε καὶ ἀμφίπολοι δύ’ ἕποντο,
Αἴθρη Πιτθῆος θυγάτηρ, Κλυμένη τε βοῶπις·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ argennēisi kalypsamenē othonēisin
hormat’ ek thalamoio teren kata dakry cheousa
ouk oiē, hama tēi ge kai amphipoloi dy’ heponto,
Aithrē Pitthēos thygatēr, Klymenē te boōpis·
sentences.l:
And at once, with white linen having veiled herself,
she set out from the chamber, down a tender tear shedding,
not alone; with her, indeed, two handmaids also followed,
Aethra, daughter of Pittheus, and ox-eyed Clymene;
sentences.i: At once she veiled herself in white linen and set out from her chamber, shedding tender tears. She was not alone; two handmaids went with her, Aethra, the daughter of Pittheus, and ox-eyed Clymene;
sentences.n: ἀργεννῇσι ὀθόνῃσιν is ‘white linen’, in the epic dative plural -ῃσι, and καλυψαμένη is the aorist middle participle of καλύπτω, ‘having covered herself’, so ‘veiled’. ὁρμᾶτ’ is ὁρμᾶτο, the imperfect of ὁρμάομαι ‘set out’, and ἐκ θαλάμοιο is ‘from the chamber’ (epic genitive -οιο). τέρεν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα is ‘a tender tear shedding down’, κατά in tmesis with χέουσα. Line 143 is word for word a line of the Odyssey; ἅμα τῇ γε is ‘with her, indeed’, ἀμφίπολοι ‘handmaids’ and δύ’ is δύο ‘two’; ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The names that follow, in apposition, are the two handmaids; βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵκανον ὅθι Σκαιαὶ πύλαι ἦσαν.
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ epeith’ hikanon hothi Skaiai pylai ēsan.
sentences.l: And quickly then they came to where the Scaean Gates were.
sentences.i: Then they quickly came to the place where the Scaean Gates were.
sentences.n: αἶψα ‘quickly’ and ἔπειτ’ ‘then’ run the journey together. ἵκανον is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, and ὅθι is ‘where’. Σκαιαὶ πύλαι are the Scaean Gates, the gate of Troy at which the old men sit; the meaning of Σκαιαί is not certain, and ‘left-hand’ (from σκαιός) is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀμφὶ Πρίαμον καὶ Πάνθοον ἠδὲ Θυμοίτην
Λάμπόν τε Κλυτίον θ’ Ἱκετάονά τ’ ὄζον Ἄρηος
Οὐκαλέγων τε καὶ Ἀντήνωρ πεπνυμένω ἄμφω
ἥατο δημογέροντες ἐπὶ Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσι,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ amphi Priamon kai Panthoon ēde Thymoitēn
Lampon te Klytion th’ Hiketaona t’ ozon Arēos
Oukalegōn te kai Antēnōr pepnymenō amphō
hēato dēmogerontes epi Skaiēisi pylēisi,
sentences.l:
And they, around Priam and Panthous and Thymoetes,
Lampus and Clytius and Hicetaon, scion of Ares,
and Ucalegon and Antenor, the two prudent,
sat, elders of the people, at the Scaean Gates,
sentences.i: There, around Priam and Panthous and Thymoetes, Lampus and Clytius and Hicetaon, scion of Ares, and Ucalegon and Antenor, both prudent men, sat the elders of the people at the Scaean Gates,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the old men, the subject of ἥατο, an epic form of ἧντο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; the main clause is held back to the end of the sentence. ἀμφί with the accusative is ‘around’, and the names that follow are the other elders: Panthous, Thymoetes, Lampus, Clytius, Hicetaon, Ucalegon and Antenor. ὄζον Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is a branch-word used of a descendant, as in the Catalogue. πεπνυμένω ἄμφω is dual, ‘both prudent’, of Ucalegon and Antenor. δημογέροντες is ‘elders of the people’ (δῆμος ‘people’ + γέρων ‘old man’), and Σκαιῇσι πύλῃσι is the epic dative plural. Line 146 is metrically irregular as transmitted, at the name Θυμοίτην: it scans only if the υ of its first syllable is counted short.

sentences.t:
γήραϊ δὴ πολέμοιο πεπαυμένοι, ἀλλ’ ἀγορηταὶ
ἐσθλοί, τεττίγεσσιν ἐοικότες οἵ τε καθ’ ὕλην
δενδρέῳ ἐφεζόμενοι ὄπα λειριόεσσαν ἱεῖσι·
sentences.tr:
gēraï dē polemoio pepaumenoi, all’ agorētai
esthloi, tettigessin eoikotes hoi te kath’ hylēn
dendreōi ephezomenoi opa leirioessan hieisi·
sentences.i: They had given up fighting because of old age, but they were good speakers, like the cicadas that sit on a tree in the forest and send out their lily-like voice;
sentences.n: γήραϊ is the epic uncontracted dative of γῆρας ‘old age’, the cause; πεπαυμένοι is the perfect participle of παύω in the middle, ‘having ceased’, with the genitive πολέμοιο ‘from war’. ἀγορηταὶ ἐσθλοί is ‘good speakers’. τεττίγεσσιν ἐοικότες is ‘like cicadas’ (ἐοικότες, the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, takes the dative). οἵ τε is ‘which’, καθ’ ὕλην ‘in the forest’, and δενδρέῳ ἐφεζόμενοι ‘sitting on a tree’. ἱεῖσι is ‘send out’, the present of ἵημι, and ὄπα is the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’. λειριόεσσαν is ‘lily-like’, from λείριον ‘lily’; what the likeness is, the pale delicacy or the clearness of the voice, is not certain, and the English keeps the root.

sentences.t: τοῖοι ἄρα Τρώων ἡγήτορες ἧντ’ ἐπὶ πύργῳ.
sentences.tr: toioi ara Trōōn hēgētores hēnt’ epi pyrgōi.
sentences.l: Of such a kind, then, the leaders of the Trojans were sitting on the tower.
sentences.i: Such were the leaders of the Trojans who sat on the tower.
sentences.n: τοῖοι ἄρα is ‘of such a kind, then’, answering the comparison with the cicadas. ἡγήτορες is ‘leaders’, and ἧντ’ is ἧντο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ἐπὶ πύργῳ ‘on the tower’ is the tower at the Scaean Gates, where these men sit (149).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὡς οὖν εἴδονθ’ Ἑλένην ἐπὶ πύργον ἰοῦσαν,
ἦκα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευον·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hōs oun eidonth’ Helenēn epi pyrgon iousan,
ēka pros allēlous epea pteroent’ agoreuon·
sentences.l:
And they, when then they saw Helen coming to the tower,
softly to one another winged words spoke;
sentences.i: And when they saw Helen coming to the tower, they spoke winged words softly to one another:
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὡς οὖν is ‘and they, when then’. εἴδονθ’ is εἴδοντο, an aorist middle of εἶδον ‘saw’ with an active sense, and ἰοῦσαν is the participle of εἶμι, ‘coming, going’. ἦκα is ‘softly’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα are the stock ‘winged words’, and ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω, ‘they spoke’, here in private talk and not in an assembly.

sentences.t:
οὐ νέμεσις Τρῶας καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιοὺς
τοιῇδ’ ἀμφὶ γυναικὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἄλγεα πάσχειν·
sentences.tr:
ou nemesis Trōas kai eÿknēmidas Achaious
toiēid’ amphi gynaiki polyn chronon algea paschein·
sentences.l:
“No resentment is it, that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans
for such a woman a long time suffer pains;
sentences.i: “It is no cause for resentment that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans suffer pains so long over such a woman;
sentences.n: οὐ νέμεσις is ‘there is no resentment’ (no cause for it), and the accusative Τρῶας καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς with the infinitive πάσχειν gives what is not to be resented: ‘that Trojans and well-greaved Achaeans suffer’. τοιῇδ’ ἀμφὶ γυναικί is ‘for (over) such a woman’, πολὺν χρόνον ‘a long time’, and ἄλγεα ‘pains’.

sentences.t: αἰνῶς ἀθανάτῃσι θεῇς εἰς ὦπα ἔοικεν·
sentences.tr: ainōs athanatēisi theēis eis ōpa eoiken·
sentences.l: dreadfully, to immortal goddesses, in face she is like;
sentences.i: she is dreadfully like the immortal goddesses to look at;
sentences.n: αἰνῶς is ‘dreadfully’, the adverb of αἰνός ‘dread’, used to strengthen: ‘terribly like’. ἀθανάτῃσι θεῇς is the epic dative plural, ‘to immortal goddesses’, with ἔοικεν ‘is like’; εἰς ὦπα is ‘to the face’, ὦπα being the accusative of ὤψ ‘face, look’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς τοίη περ ἐοῦσ’ ἐν νηυσὶ νεέσθω,
μηδ’ ἡμῖν τεκέεσσί τ’ ὀπίσσω πῆμα λίποιτο.
sentences.tr:
alla kai hōs toiē per eous’ en nēusi neesthō,
mēd’ hēmin tekeessi t’ opissō pēma lipoito.
sentences.l:
but even so, such a one though she is, in the ships let her go back,
and not to us and to our children hereafter a woe be left.”
sentences.i: but even so, such as she is, let her go back in the ships, and let no woe be left to us and to our children hereafter.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’ (ὧς = οὕτως), and τοίη περ ἐοῦσ’ is ‘such a one though she is’, περ making it concessive. νεέσθω is the imperative of νέομαι ‘go back’, ἐν νηυσί ‘in the ships’. μηδ’ … πῆμα λίποιτο is a wish, ‘and let no woe be left’: λίποιτο is the aorist middle optative of λείπω ‘leave’, with the dative ἡμῖν τεκέεσσί τ’ ‘to us and to our children’ (τεκέεσσι the epic dative plural of τέκος), and ὀπίσσω ‘hereafter’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, Πρίαμος δ’ Ἑλένην ἐκαλέσσατο φωνῇ·
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephan, Priamos d’ Helenēn ekalessato phōnēi·
sentences.l: So then they spoke, and Priam called Helen to him with his voice;
sentences.i: So they spoke, and Priam called Helen to him aloud;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so then they spoke’, ἔφαν being ἔφασαν. ἐκαλέσσατο is the aorist middle of καλέω, ‘called to himself’, with the epic doubled σσ, and φωνῇ is ‘with his voice’, ‘aloud’. Priam sits among the elders (146), so this follows what they have just said.

sentences.t:
δεῦρο πάροιθ’ ἐλθοῦσα φίλον τέκος ἵζευ ἐμεῖο,
ὄφρα ἴδῃ πρότερόν τε πόσιν πηούς τε φίλους τε·
sentences.tr:
deuro paroith’ elthousa philon tekos hizeu emeio,
ophra idēi proteron te posin pēous te philous te·
sentences.l:
“Here, having come forward, dear child, sit down by me,
that you may see your former husband and kinsmen and friends;
sentences.i: “Come here, dear child, and sit down by me, so that you may see your former husband and your kinsmen and friends;
sentences.n: δεῦρο … ἐλθοῦσα is ‘having come here’, an aorist participle that works like a command with ἵζευ (the imperative of ἵζομαι ‘sit down’); πάροιθ’ is ‘forward, to the front’, and ἐμεῖο, the epic genitive of ἐγώ, goes with ἵζευ (‘by me’) or with πάροιθ’ (‘in front of me’). φίλον τέκος is ‘dear child’. ὄφρα ἴδῃ is ‘so that you may see’, ἴδῃ being the contracted second-person middle subjunctive (see ἴδηαι at 130). πρότερον ‘former’ goes with πόσιν ‘husband’, and πηούς are relatives by marriage.

sentences.t:
οὔ τί μοι αἰτίη ἐσσί, θεοί νύ μοι αἴτιοί εἰσιν
οἵ μοι ἐφώρμησαν πόλεμον πολύδακρυν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
ou ti moi aitiē essi, theoi ny moi aitioi eisin
hoi moi ephōrmēsan polemon polydakryn Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
You are not at all to blame to me; the gods, indeed, to me are to blame,
who stirred up against me the tearful war of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: In my eyes you are in no way to blame; it is the gods who are to blame, they who stirred up against me the tearful war of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: αἰτίη is a noun, ‘cause, blame’, used as a predicate with ἐσσί (the epic second person of εἰμί), so ‘you are to blame’; αἴτιοί is the adjective ‘responsible’, said of the gods. μοι is a dative of reference, ‘in my view’, and νύ is a particle of emphasis. ἐφώρμησαν is the aorist of ἐφορμάω, ‘set on, stir up’, with μοι ‘against me’. πολύδακρυν ‘tearful’ is the epithet of 132 again, and Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’ is the war that they wage.

sentences.t:
ὥς μοι καὶ τόνδ’ ἄνδρα πελώριον ἐξονομήνῃς
ὅς τις ὅδ’ ἐστὶν Ἀχαιὸς ἀνὴρ ἠΰς τε μέγας τε.
sentences.tr:
hōs moi kai tond’ andra pelōrion exonomēnēis
hos tis hod’ estin Achaios anēr ēÿs te megas te.
sentences.l:
so that for me this man too, huge, you may name,
who this one is, the Achaean man, both good and great.
sentences.i: so that you may also tell me the name of this huge man, who this Achaean is, both good and great.
sentences.n: ὥς is ὡς ‘so that’, with the aorist subjunctive ἐξονομήνῃς ‘you may name’ (ἐξονομαίνω ‘call by name’), and μοι καί … τόνδ’ ἄνδρα is ‘for me also this man’, a further request after the seeing of 162–163. πελώριον ‘huge’ is an adjective of size and wonder. ὅς τις ὅδ’ ἐστίν is an indirect question, ‘who this one is’, and ἠΰς τε μέγας τε is ‘both good and great’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι μὲν κεφαλῇ καὶ μείζονες ἄλλοι ἔασι,
καλὸν δ’ οὕτω ἐγὼν οὔ πω ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
οὐδ’ οὕτω γεραρόν·
sentences.tr:
ētoi men kephalēi kai meizones alloi easi,
kalon d’ houtō egōn ou pō idon ophthalmoisin,
oud’ houtō geraron·
sentences.i: Others are indeed taller by a head, but I have never yet seen with my eyes one so fine, or one so stately;
sentences.n: ἤτοι is printed as one word, ‘indeed’, and μέν answers the δέ of the next line. κεφαλῇ is a dative of measure, ‘by a head’, καί ‘even’, and ἔασι is the epic form of εἰσί. καλόν and γεραρόν are neuter adjectives with no noun, ‘a fine (thing)’, ‘a stately (thing)’, standing for a person; ἐγών is a longer form of ἐγώ ‘I’, ἴδον an unaugmented aorist of ‘see’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν the epic dative plural of ὀφθαλμός ‘eye’. οὕτω is ‘so’, and οὔ πω ‘not yet’. γεραρός is ‘stately, venerable’.

sentences.t: βασιλῆϊ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικε.
sentences.tr: basilēï gar andri eoike.
sentences.l: for to a man, a king, he is like.”
sentences.i: for he looks like a king.”
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for ‘stately’. βασιλῆϊ is the epic dative of βασιλεύς ‘king’, with ἀνδρί ‘man’ in apposition, and ἔοικε ‘is like’ takes the dative. The speech, and the part, end here.
